processing: Sun-dried leaf is steamed, kneaded, pressed into a rounded melon shape and dried. This follows the general tribute-tea craft recorded for Ning'er; modern pieces may vary by maker.
harvest_season: Not tied to a documented picking. For modern pieces, ask the maker about the leaf and year.
appearance_dry: A rounded, melon-like block of pressed leaf, ranging from dark in old pieces to greener in young ones.
appearance_liquor: Golden to amber in young raw pieces, and darker with age.
appearance_wet: Whole or broken pressed leaf, varying a great deal with the maker.
taste_profile: Modern pieces vary too much for one description. They generally taste like raw pu-erh of the same age, with the slow change that tight pressing brings.

brewing.notes: Dense pressing makes it hard to break, so pry a piece off the side with a pick. Allow extra time for the first steeps to open up.

vintage_note: Sold today by year and maker as a modern shape, and the historic tribute pieces are museum objects, never sold as tea to drink. Claims of great age deserve scepticism. Tight melons also age slowly, as dense shapes do.
description:
Jingua Gongcha, golden melon tribute tea, is pu-erh pressed into a rounded melon shape. Its fame comes from the Qing tribute story and from old pieces kept in museums.

The shape is the defining feature. It is a very dense mass with little exposed surface, so it ages more slowly than a flat cake.

A modern melon is usually an ordinary raw pu-erh in a striking shape. It is awkward to break and is often bought for display, so choose one by the leaf it contains, and do not pay for the name.

Treat tribute claims on a modern piece as marketing. Factories have made their own versions for years, including the Kunming factory's Jixing brand, and nothing about the shape ties a piece to the imperial originals.
history:
Pu-erh was listed as a tribute tea in the Qing dynasty, and an official tea bureau handled it, according to China's intangible heritage record for Ning'er tribute tea craft. It is said that only two genuine old pieces survive, one in Beijing's Palace Museum and one at the Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences in Hangzhou, though this comes from popular writing.

The same popular account says the tea returned to Pu'er city in 2007. In the state-factory era, the Kunming Tea Factory listed Jixing Jingua Gongcha among its representative export products.
